key_results: A causal sinusoid can be generated as the impulse response of a second-order resonator; combining sine and cosine sections into the coupled form uses only the pole components a and b rather than a²+b², improving coefficient quantization. Periodic waveforms are impulse responses of N(z)/(1−z^(−D)), while a wavetable and circular pointer provide the lower-overhead realization. [§§16.1.1–16.1.3, Eqs. 16.1.1–16.1.22]

Adding a delayed copy gives the FIR comb H(z)=1+az^(−D), with spectral peaks separated by fs/D; feeding the delayed output back gives the IIR comb H(z)=1/(1−az^(−D)). Its epsilon-level decay time is neff=D ln(epsilon)/ln(a), or tau_eff=TD ln(epsilon)/ln(a). [§16.2.1, Eqs. 16.2.1–16.2.16]

Flanging and chorusing are time-varying delay effects: y(n)=x(n)+a x(n−d(n)). Short periodic delay modulation moves the comb notches; chorusing uses a nonzero base delay and often several independently modulated voices, whereas phasing realizes moving notches with time-varying allpass sections. [§16.2.2, Eq. 16.2.17 and surrounding algorithms]

A realistic reverberator separates direct sound, sparse early reflections, and dense late reflections. Schroeder structures build density from comb/allpass sections; putting a lowpass G(z) in the feedback loop makes high-frequency poles shorter and their transients decay faster, with approximate pole radius |G(omega_i)|^(1/D). Stability is guaranteed by |G(omega)|<1. [§16.2.3, Eqs. 16.2.32–16.2.39]

The Karplus–Strong plucked-string model initializes a delay line with noise and recirculates it through G(z)=(1+z^(−1))/2. Choosing D≈fs/f1 fixes pitch, while repeated lowpass passes make high frequencies decay faster in a natural string-like way. [§16.2.3, Eq. 16.2.40]

Compressor/expander gain is driven by a smoothed level c_n=lambda c_(n−1)+(1−lambda)|x_n|, with lambda=epsilon^(Ts/t_eff). Piecewise power-law gain functions implement compression or expansion above/below a threshold; limiters and gates are extreme ratios. [§§16.3.1–16.3.2, Eqs. 16.3.1–16.3.8]

Separate attack and release constants are obtained by switching lambda according to whether the detected level rises or falls. Smoothing the nonlinear gain and optionally delaying the signal suppresses overshoot; a side-chain supports ducking and filtered side-chains support de-essing. [§16.3.3, Eqs. 16.3.9–16.3.13]

A high-order peaking equalizer is obtained by designing a Butterworth, Chebyshev-1, Chebyshev-2, or elliptic analog lowpass shelf and applying s=(1−2 cos(omega0)z^(−1)+z^(−2))/(1−z^(−2)). The mapping sends equalizer bandedges to ±Omega_B and turns analog order N into digital order 2N. [§§17.1–17.2, Eqs. 17.2.2–17.2.18]

The prototype magnitude |Ha|²=(G²+G0² epsilon² FN²)/(1+epsilon² FN²) meets bandwidth gain GB when epsilon=sqrt((G²−GB²)/(GB²−G0²)). Choosing left-half-plane roots makes the design minimum phase, so equal-and-opposite boost and cut designs are exact inverses when their gain specifications are reciprocals. [§§17.2–17.4 and §17.6, Eqs. 17.2.10–17.2.16 and 17.6.5–17.6.7]

When both passband and secondary stopband widths are specified, Butterworth and Chebyshev order formulas follow directly from the normalized bandwidth and gain ratios, while the elliptic order uses quarter-period ratios and is rounded upward; the rounding slightly improves one specification. [§17.5, Eqs. 17.5.1–17.5.5]

Digital octave bandwidth is warped and generally asymmetric around a high center frequency. The exact equation is solved by a rapidly convergent iteration initialized by B≈(omega0/sin omega0)b; a separate remapping lets the designer state a conventional 3-dB width while retaining Chebyshev/elliptic ripple specifications. [§17.6, Eqs. 17.6.8–17.6.15]

Frequency-shifted transposed, normalized-lattice, and minimum-noise state-space realizations expose different numerical tradeoffs. The latter two have scaling and roundoff advantages for low center frequencies or rapidly varying parameters; weighted-arithmetic-mean bandwidth permits a fully decoupled realization whose gain, bandwidth, and center-frequency coefficients are independently controlled. [§§17.7–17.8, Eqs. 17.7.1–17.8.8]

In time-varying equalizer tests, transposed, normalized-lattice, and state-space forms remain comparable while the canonical form develops large oscillations from unscaled states. Turning gain on gradually removes overshoot; the text recommends the transposed form as a strong cost/robustness compromise. [§17.9, Figs. 17.9.6–17.9.7]

The STFT forms overlapping length-N frames separated by hop R, windows each, and computes an N-point DFT. For input length Lx, M=floor(Lx/R) and zero extension to MR+N gives M+1 complete frames; spectrogram axes are f_k=kfs/N and t_m=mR/fs. [§§18.2–18.3, Eqs. 18.2.1–18.3.1]

Inverse-frame division by a small window is numerically unsafe. Overlap-add instead yields y(n)=x(n) w_tilde(n); exact reconstruction divides by the overlapped window, while the COLA condition W(2pi r/R)=0 for r=1,…,R−1 makes w_tilde constant. [§18.4, Eqs. 18.4.1–18.4.6]

An STFT processing system may use distinct analysis and synthesis hops: analyze, transform X_km into Y_km, inverse-transform, apply a synthesis window, and overlap-add. The middle transform can implement filtering, denoising, gain control, fading, or phase modification. [§§18.5–18.6, Eqs. 18.5.1–18.6.4]

The phase vocoder preserves STFT magnitudes but estimates each bin's instantaneous-frequency offset from the modulo-2pi phase increment, Delta omega=(1/Ra)[Phi_km−Phi_k,m−1−Ra omega_k]_mod2pi, then advances synthesis phase by Rs(omega_k+Delta omega). [§§18.7 and 18.9, Eqs. 18.7.1–18.7.3 and 18.9.8–18.9.10]

Time-scale modification follows from the hop ratio r=Ra/Rs: duration changes while phase propagation preserves frequency content. Pitch scaling without duration change composes resampling with reciprocal phase-vocoder time scaling; pitch scaling is multiplicative f→rf, not additive frequency translation. [§§18.8–18.10, Eq. 18.8.1 and Fig. 18.10.1]

The normalized type-2 DCT is an orthogonal matrix transform D=Ax with inverse x=A^T D and Parseval identity ||x||²=||D||². Even extension converts it to a 2N-point FFT, yielding a fast forward and exactly reversible inverse algorithm. [§19.2, Eqs. 19.2.1–19.2.15]

DCT compression works because smooth signal blocks concentrate energy into relatively few coefficients. One method keeps a fixed count of largest coefficients per frame; another zeros every coefficient below a global fraction of the maximum. The true storage cost must include coefficient locations as well as values. [§19.3, Eqs. 19.3.1–19.3.2]

The MDCT maps 2N samples to N coefficients and is not invertible on one block: its IMDCT returns antisymmetrized/symmetrized half-blocks. With 50% overlap, the alias term from one block has the opposite sign in the next, so overlap-add cancels it and recovers the shared N samples exactly. [§19.4, Eqs. 19.4.1–19.4.8]

A symmetric length-2N analysis/synthesis window preserves TDAC when w_n²+w_(n+N)²=2 in the book's normalization. Sine and Vorbis windows satisfy this directly; cumulative sums of a symmetric seed window generate a general family including the KBD window used in AAC and AC-3. [§19.5, Eqs. 19.5.1–19.5.8]

The complete MDCT compression chain is 50%-overlapped framing, Princen–Bradley windowing, MDCT thresholding, IMDCT, a second window, and overlap-add. Boundary samples require padding or special handling because only interior half-blocks participate in TDAC. [§19.6, Eq. 19.6.10]

A multiresolution analysis is a nested sequence V_j whose orthonormal basis functions are scaled/translated copies phi_jn(t)=2^(j/2)phi(2^j t−n). A finite-resolution signal decomposes into one coarse projection plus mutually orthogonal detail spaces, and the mapping from finest samples to coarse/detail coefficients is the DWT. [§20.1, Eqs. 20.1.1–20.1.16]

Nesting V_j inside V_(j+1) forces two-scale dilation equations for the scaling and wavelet functions. Their filter coefficients h and g generate the analysis/synthesis relations that underlie Mallat's pyramid; choosing g as the conjugate mirror of h supplies the orthogonal detail branch. [§20.2, Eqs. 20.2.1–20.2.14]

Orthonormality requires even-shift correlations equal to Kronecker deltas and the quadrature identity |H(omega)|²+|H(omega+pi)|²=2. Daubechies D_K filters have length 2K and K Nyquist zeros; equivalently the wavelet has K vanishing moments and annihilates polynomials through degree K−1. [§20.3, Eqs. 20.3.1–20.3.20]

Mallat analysis filters with time-reversed lowpass/highpass filters and downsamples; synthesis upsamples and filters with h and g. Downsampling aliases each subband, but the quadrature conditions make the complete two-channel bank perfectly reconstructing. [§20.4, Eqs. 20.4.4–20.4.15]

The periodized DWT can be expressed as an orthogonal matrix w=W^T x, x=Ww, or as circular-convolution filter-bank stages. It stores exactly N coefficients and costs O(MN), linear in signal length for fixed filter order M; package outputs can differ by signs and cyclic shifts without representing a different transform. [§20.5, Eqs. 20.5.1–20.5.23]

Wavelet denoising transforms, thresholds only detail coefficients, and inverts. Hard thresholding deletes small coefficients; soft thresholding also shrinks survivors and is the exact solution of an L2 data-fit plus L1 wavelet penalty. VisuShrink uses lambda=sigma sqrt(2 log2 N), with sigma estimated robustly from finest-scale details. [§20.7, Eqs. 20.7.1–20.7.8]

The undecimated wavelet transform removes all downsamplers and instead uses successively dilated à-trous filters. It is redundant and costs O(N log N), but remains perfectly reconstructing through the half-sum identity and is shift invariant; the source's benchmark shows better denoising than the ordinary DWT. [§20.8, Eqs. 20.8.1–20.8.8 and Fig. 20.8.6]

For a continuous-time transfer function with direct feedthrough, initial conditions immediately before and after t=0 need not agree. Up to second order, y(0+)=y(0−)+b0x(0+) and y_dot(0+)=y_dot(0−)+b0x_dot(0+)+(b1−a1b0)x(0+); these mappings reconcile Laplace zero-input/zero-state and classical homogeneous/forced solutions. [§§21.2–21.4, Eqs. 21.2.1–21.4.4]

Forward Euler, backward Euler, and trapezoidal discretization are one substitution family s=(1−z^(−1))/(p+qz^(−1)): (p,q)=(0,T), (T,0), and (T/2,T/2). Substituting into Ha(s) gives explicit first- and second-order coefficient maps. [§21.8, Eqs. 21.8.1–21.8.5]

Zero-order hold is Hd(z)=(1−z^(−1)) Z{Ha(s)/s}; first-order hold is Hd(z)=((1−z^(−1))²/(Tz^(−1))) Z{Ha(s)/s²}. Partial fractions turn these definitions into exact pole mappings z=e^(pT) and implementable first-/second-order difference equations. [§21.9, Eqs. 21.9.1–21.9.15]

Real-time implementation iterates the difference equation sample by sample. For a second-order system initialized from continuous-time conditions, y_(−1)≈y(0−) and y_(−2)≈y(0−)−T y_dot(0−); a third-order initialization also uses T² y_double_dot(0−). [§§21.7 and 21.10–21.11, Eqs. 21.7.3–21.7.8]

The zero-order hold is step invariant: the digital step response equals samples of the analog step response. Its impulse response equals the integral of h_a over the preceding sample interval; conventional impulse invariance h_d(n)≈T h_a(nT) is only a small-T approximation and needs a half-weight correction at n=0 for causal discontinuities. [§§21.14–21.15, Eqs. 21.14.14–21.15.5]

First-order hold linearly interpolates the input over each sampling interval and is ramp invariant. For a pure integrator, ZOH reduces to forward Euler while FOH reduces to the trapezoidal rule, unifying the hold and numerical-integration viewpoints. [§§21.16–21.17, Eqs. 21.16.1–21.17.1]

For negative feedback with plant G and controller Gc, the reference, error, and disturbance paths share denominator 1+GcG: H=GcG/(1+GcG), Herr=1/(1+GcG), and Hdist=G/(1+GcG). This makes tracking, disturbance rejection, and closed-loop pole placement one algebraic problem. [§22.1, Eqs. 22.1.2–22.1.3]

A PID controller Gc=kp+ki/s+kd s trades rise time, overshoot, and settling time. The final-value theorem exposes steady-state error; in the presented plants a nonzero integral term is required for zero step and ramp tracking error. [§22.2, Eqs. 22.2.1–22.2.2]

A digital loop must include the hold-plus-plant equivalent Gd(z), not merely substitute z into the analog closed loop. A practical digital PID uses trapezoidal integration and backward-Euler differentiation: kp+(kiT/2)(1+z^(−1))/(1−z^(−1))+(kd/T)(1−z^(−1)). [§22.3, Eqs. 22.3.1–22.3.4]

The examples progress from linear cruise and antenna plants to an inverted pendulum and a genuinely nonlinear on/off thermostat. The thermostat is simulated by forward time stepping with a discontinuous furnace control R(n)=R0 when T(n)<Tc(n), showing why a difference equation can be more useful than a closed-form transfer function. [§§22.4.1–22.4.4, Eqs. 22.4.29–22.4.35]

Local polynomial smoothing fits y≈Sc by least squares, giving c=(S^T S)^(−1)S^T y and fitted samples y_hat=By with B=S(S^T S)^(−1)S^T. B is a symmetric idempotent orthogonal projector; its columns are position-specific smoothing filters that handle the two boundaries without padding. [§§23.2–23.4, Eqs. 23.2.2–23.2.16]

The central filter is simultaneously the least-squares polynomial fit and the minimum-noise-reduction-ratio filter subject to moment constraints sum n^i b(n)=delta_i. Those constraints preserve polynomial inputs and signal moments through degree d and are equivalent to d derivatives of a flat frequency response at DC. [§23.8, Eqs. 23.8.1–23.8.21]

Evaluating the fitted polynomial away from the center yields predictive/interpolating FIR filters; differentiating it yields minimum-norm derivative filters. A Farrow structure factors the continuously variable delay parameter into polynomial powers while fixed subfilters process the samples. [§§23.6–23.7 and 23.9, Eqs. 23.6.1–23.9.11]

Higher polynomial degree preserves more high-frequency detail but passes more noise: asymptotically the quadratic/cubic and quartic/quintic central filters have NRR about 2.25/N and 3.52/N, versus 1/N for the averager. [§23.8, Eqs. 23.8.2–23.8.3]

Weighted local polynomial fits lead to minimum-roughness filters when the quadratic noise metric is prefiltered by a difference operator D(z)=(1−z^(−1))^s. Henderson filters and Hahn orthogonal polynomials provide closed, computationally stable representations of this family. [§§23.11–23.13, Eqs. 23.11.1–23.11.30]

Missing samples and known outliers are handled by assigning them zero weight, estimating them from surrounding samples, and then smoothing the adjusted record. Robust filtering automates this with iterated bisquare weights derived from median-scaled residuals; 3–4 iterations are usually adequate. [§23.15, Eqs. 23.15.1–23.15.10]

For unequally spaced observations, a local bandwidth h_t selects neighbors and a compact window weights them; the local weighted normal equations return value, slope, and higher derivatives. Fixed bandwidth keeps h constant while nearest-neighbor bandwidth keeps the local sample count constant, exposing the bias–variance tradeoff directly. [§23.16, Eqs. 23.16.1–23.16.28]

Leave-one-out cross-validation can be computed without N refits: x_hat_(−i)=(x_hat_i−H_ii y_i)/(1−H_ii), so CV averages ((y_i−x_hat_i)/(1−H_ii))². GCV replaces H_ii by tr(H)/N; both are useful guides but the ethanol example shows their optimum may visibly undersmooth. [§23.17, Eqs. 23.17.1–23.17.9; §23.18, Figs. 23.18.4–23.18.5]

Adaptive local polynomial smoothing estimates normalized curvature and shrinks bandwidth where curvature is high, preserving benchmark peaks and discontinuities that a fixed bandwidth broadens. Repeated observations are exactly reducible to their average with the local weight multiplied by their multiplicity; LOESS adds nearest-neighbor tricube fits and iterative robustness weights. [§§23.19–23.21, Eqs. 23.19.1–23.21.2]
pedagogy: A computational, derivation-heavy application block that repeatedly turns a physical or statistical story into a transfer function, an explicit sample-processing loop, and runnable MATLAB. The chapters usually begin with a concrete engineering failure or need—echo density, changing audio frequency content, blocking artifacts, multiscale detail, analog-system deployment, feedback tracking, or oversmoothing—and then derive the remedy through algebra and block diagrams. Proof style is constructive: pole/zero factorization, matrix identities, projection geometry, normal equations, partial fractions, and polyphase/filter-bank manipulations are carried far enough to yield implementation formulas. Examples use numerical coefficients and often compare several structures or parameter choices rather than displaying one ideal answer. Exercises are unusually project-like: Chapter 16 has 25 problems dominated by C/MATLAB audio effects and listening tests; Chapters 18–20 require complete STFT/phase-vocoder, DCT/MDCT, and wavelet implementations; Chapter 21 checks analytic, lsim, and discretized solutions against one another; Chapter 22 develops four control case studies; Chapter 23 ends with only two formal problems because most of its 102 pages embed worked derivations, datasets, and function implementations in the prose. Prerequisites are substantial: LTI systems, z/Laplace transforms, DFT/FFT, FIR/IIR structures, filter design, linear algebra and least squares, probability/noise, differential equations, and basic MATLAB. The most transferable teaching move is cross-validation among representations: the same result is shown as a physical model, equation, pole/zero or matrix property, block diagram, code, and numerical plot.

gems: The DTMF example turns a keypad press into two parallel cosine resonators and then reverses the question at the receiver: recover one row frequency and one column frequency by an eight-filter bank or selected DFT bins. [§16.1.1, Example 16.1.1 and Figs. 16.1.3–16.1.4]

A simple echo and a simple reverberator differ only in which side of the delay is fed back, yet that small structural move changes a two-impulse FIR into an infinite, exponentially decaying room-like response. [§16.2.1, Figs. 16.2.2 and 16.2.6]
The chapter makes a memorable exception to ordinary DSP priorities: reverberation is valuable precisely for its transient, not its steady state. [§16.2.3]

The compressor section punctures the slogan that compression amplifies weak sounds: in the presented feedforward curve it attenuates only strong sounds, but the reduced overall dynamic range is perceived as if weak sounds grew. [§16.3.2, discussion after Figs. 16.3.3–16.3.4]

The ducker experiment uses speech as a side-chain to push music down only while someone talks, then asks the learner to tune attack, release, threshold, and ratio by listening rather than by a single numerical score. [§16.3.4, Experiment 2 and Eq. 16.3.15]

A five-iteration Landen implementation is enough for elliptic equalizer response error below 10^−5 percent, making the apparently exotic elliptic case only slightly more complicated than Chebyshev in practice. [§17.9, discussion after Fig. 17.9.4]

Changing equalizer gain in one jump produces overshoot, while as few as two intermediate gain steps largely remove it—a small control insight hidden inside an audio filter realization comparison. [§17.9, Fig. 17.9.7]

The phase-vocoder derivation explains phase unwrapping as measuring the deviation from the phase advance a DFT bin should have had, rather than as an arbitrary numerical cleanup. [§18.9, Eqs. 18.9.7–18.9.10]

The pitch-shift exercise asks for both listening evidence and spectral evidence on a flute, then traces a four-millisecond waveform through resampling, chipmunk playback, and duration restoration. [§18.11, Pitch-Scale Modification]
MDCT reconstruction is deliberately wrong block by block; exactness emerges only because adjacent wrong answers carry equal and opposite time-domain aliases. [§19.4, Eqs. 19.4.2–19.4.4]

The MDCT debugging table lists every overlapping IMDCT contribution for x=1,…,28; rows 5–24 add to exact integers even though the individual frame contributions look wildly aliased. [§19.6, MDCT/TDAC experiment]

The same four bumps/blocks/HeaviSine/Doppler signals appear in both the wavelet and local-polynomial chapters, creating a rare within-book head-to-head comparison rather than isolated success plots. [§20.7, Fig. 20.7.1; §23.19, Figs. 23.19.1–23.19.4]

A single eight-sample vector is carried through matrix DWT, convolutional DWT, multiple software packages, and exact inverse reconstruction; the differing sign/order conventions make implementation equivalence visible instead of hand-waved. [§20.5]

ZOH, forward Euler, FOH, trapezoidal integration, step invariance, and ramp invariance are shown as different faces of the same sampled-system construction rather than a list of unrelated recipes. [§§21.14–21.17]

The initial-condition mapping explains a subtle discontinuity: a causal input step can make y(0+) differ from y(0−) whenever the transfer function has direct feedthrough, even though the system itself is finite and causal. [§21.2, Eq. 21.2.1]

The control chapter escalates gracefully from car speed to radar antenna to inverted pendulum to bang-bang home heating, moving from clean linear transfer functions to a nonlinear simulation without changing the feedback story. [§22.4]

Local polynomial filters are presented as a recurring rediscovery: Schiaparelli in 1866, De Forest in 1871, actuarial graduation, Savitzky–Golay spectroscopy, and Henderson economic trend filters all solve closely related projection problems. [§23.1]

Polynomial preservation becomes peak preservation: the moment constraints retain area, centroid, and width information, which explains why Savitzky–Golay smoothing can protect narrow spectroscopic or ECG features better than a same-length averager. [§23.8, Eq. 23.8.16]

The ethanol example refuses to worship an automatic optimum: GCV chooses a visibly jagged fit, and the text recommends a nearby, slightly larger bandwidth based on judgment because the GCV minimum is broad. [§23.18, Figs. 23.18.4–23.18.5]

The motorcycle dataset contains 133 records but only 94 unique times; averaging repeats is not merely a shortcut, because weighting each average by its multiplicity is algebraically identical to fitting every observation. [§23.20, Eqs. 23.20.1–23.20.3]
